column1: # Whizbang performance baseline. One measure per line, tab separated:
#   name<TAB>value<TAB>unit<TAB>ceiling<TAB>note
# The value is what the measure read when the line was last written, and is reported as drift on
# every run. The CEILING is the gate, and is deliberately optional: a measure with no ceiling is
# recorded and never fails a run. Declare one only where the number is a property of the design
# rather than of the machine, and say why in the note -- a ceiling that encodes a machine's speed
# will either flap or hide a real regression, which is the failure mode this file exists to avoid.
# Values are WORK DONE (tuples, scans, blocks, rows), never wall clock. Time moves with the runner,
# its neighbors and its cache; a plan's page and tuple counts do not.
# Eight streams carrying 2,500 settled rows each in all three queue tables, none of them in the
# stream ledger, so every ring takes the deterministic-target branch. A ring names streams and must
# cost what it names, never what those streams have accumulated.
# Before the deterministic branch stopped recovering a stream's partition number by reading the
# queue table, the same scenario read 20,000 tuples and took one sequential scan PER RING on each
# of the three branches. That is the measurement this suite exists to have caught.
# The ceiling is on tuples read, and it is a property of the design: the partition number is a
# total function of the stream id, so a ring has no reason to read a queue row at all. A hundred
# leaves room for a planner that reads a page to answer something else while still being two orders
# of magnitude below a scan of a 20,000-row table. Scan counts are recorded without a ceiling,
# because they are the same finding counted a second way and one gate per family is enough.

column1: # --- Store emptiness probe against a pending backlog -----------------------------------------
# 200 streams carrying 100 pending unpublished outbox rows each, then a producer storing four
# messages per call on streams the outbox has never held. Before its first insert for a stream the
# store asks whether that stream has a pending row, so it knows whether to ring a doorbell.
# The ceiling is on tuples read per ROW WRITTEN, which is the ratio a deployed fleet reported at
# 4,550 and the one that makes a scan obvious whatever the absolute size of the table: a store
# should read about what it writes. Fifty leaves room for the small bookkeeping tables the store
# legitimately reads while being two orders of magnitude below a scan.
# The absolute per-call tuple count carries a ceiling too, because the ratio alone can be satisfied
# by a call that writes more rather than by one that reads less.
# Measured before the fix: 80,078 tuples and 4 sequential scans per call, 20,019.5 tuples per row
# written. Every stream_id index on wh_outbox is partial on a condition this predicate cannot
# satisfy, so nothing served it and it scanned every unpublished row to prove a fresh stream empty.
store.rows_written_per_call
store.wh_outbox.seq_scans_per_call
column5: was 4 per call before the fix, one per fresh stream

column5: was 80078; a probe by stream id must not read the table

# 100 streams and a batch of 10 at two depths: 12 pending perspective events per stream, then 200.
# Same batch, same stream count; only the depth differs.
# The gate is the MULTIPLE, because it is the only measure that separates a poll that is expensive
# because it was asked for a lot from a poll that is expensive because of what it happened to find.
# A poll bounded by the batch it was asked for holds this near one. Two leaves room for the larger
# table's own index depth while still failing a poll whose cost tracks its consumer's data shape.
# The absolute deep-stream cost carries a ceiling as well, so the multiple cannot be satisfied by
# making the shallow case worse. Rows leased per call is the mechanism rather than a gate: the
# acquisition selects a batch of STREAMS and then leases every pending event of each one.
# Measured before the fix: 3,730.5 blocks a call shallow, 54,914 deep, 1,766.7 rows leased a call
# at depth, a 14.7x multiple. Three deployed services reported 4,575, 12,022 and 29,018 blocks a
# call on this same code, which is one code path at three data shapes.
